report:
## Evidence Assessment

Your claim is well-supported, though the strength of the effect varies by study.

**Strongest evidence:** The pivotal trial is Tuuli et al.'s randomized trial (NEJM, 2016), which found chlorhexidine-alcohol resulted in significantly lower surgical-site infection (SSI) rates than iodine-alcohol after cesarean delivery ([NEJM](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048)). This large, well-designed RCT is the most-cited source underlying the claim.

**Meta-analyses generally confirm this**, though effect sizes are modest:
- A 2020 Cochrane systematic review found "moderate-certainty evidence" that chlorhexidine gluconate is "probably slightly more effective" than povidone-iodine at reducing SSI after cesarean section ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32580252/); [Cochrane](https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD007462_skin-preparation-preventing-infection-following-caesarean-section)).
- A separate systematic review/meta-analysis (2018) also supports chlorhexidine-alcohol's superiority ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/)).
- Smaller trials, such as an Indian pilot RCT, found a trend favoring chlorhexidine but did not reach statistical significance, likely due to limited sample size ([PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8369632/)).

**Some contradicting nuance:** One meta-analysis with trial sequential analysis concluded chlorhexidine showed "no additional advantage" over iodine specifically in cesarean sections, suggesting the evidence base, while favorable overall, isn't entirely uniform across all analyses ([PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28817989/)).

**Conclusion:** The claim is accurate and reflects the consensus of the best available evidence, including a landmark RCT and a Cochrane review. WHO and CDC guidelines recommend chlorhexidine-alcohol as the preferred skin antiseptic for surgical procedures, including cesarean delivery. However, the magnitude of benefit is described as "moderate" or "slight" rather than dramatic, and not every individual study reaches statistical significance—so while directionally consistent, the evidence should be framed as showing a real but modest advantage rather than an overwhelming one.
